notes.definition: The elements in Group 1 are the alkali metals (lithium, sodium, potassium, rubidium, caesium and francium). Their atoms have one electron in the outer shell, which they lose to form 1+ ions, and they become more reactive going down the group.
explanation: Group 1 elements are called the alkali metals because they react with water to form alkaline solutions. They are all metals with one electron in their outer shell, which explains why they have very similar chemical properties. They are soft enough to cut with a knife, have low densities (lithium, sodium and potassium float on water) and have low melting points compared with most metals. The melting point decreases going down the group, from lithium (181 °C) to caesium (28 °C). A freshly cut surface is shiny but quickly tarnishes as the metal reacts with oxygen, so the metals are stored under oil to keep out air and water.

With oxygen, the alkali metals form metal oxides. For example, 4Li(s) + O₂(g) → 2Li₂O(s) and 4Na(s) + O₂(g) → 2Na₂O(s). When heated, they burn with coloured flames (lithium red, sodium yellow-orange, potassium lilac). With chlorine, they react vigorously when heated to form white metal chlorides, which are ionic solids that dissolve in water: 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s). The reactions get more vigorous going down the group.

With water, the alkali metals form a metal hydroxide and hydrogen gas: 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g). The hydroxide dissolves to form an alkaline solution, so universal indicator turns purple. Lithium floats and fizzes steadily, slowly getting smaller. Sodium melts into a shiny ball, fizzes rapidly and moves around on the surface. Potassium melts, fizzes violently and the heat ignites the hydrogen, giving a lilac flame; it may spit or crackle. Rubidium and caesium react explosively.

In all these reactions the metal atom loses its single outer electron to form an ion with a 1+ charge, such as Na⁺. The ion has the stable electronic structure of a noble gas: Na (2,8,1) becomes Na⁺ (2,8). The more easily this outer electron is lost, the more reactive the metal.

Reactivity increases going down Group 1. Going down the group, each atom has an extra shell of electrons, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus. There are also more inner shells between the nucleus and the outer electron, which shield it from the positive charge of the nucleus. Even though the nucleus has more protons, the larger distance and greater shielding mean the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker. The outer electron is therefore lost more easily, so the metal reacts more vigorously.

You can use these trends to predict the properties of elements further down the group. For example, rubidium and caesium will be softer, have lower melting points and react even more violently with water, oxygen and chlorine than potassium. Their compounds have the same type of formula because all Group 1 metals form 1+ ions: RbOH, Cs₂O and CsCl.
keyFacts: Group 1 elements are the alkali metals; they have 1 electron in their outer shell.
They lose the outer electron to form 1+ ions, for example Li⁺, Na⁺, K⁺.
Reactivity increases going down the group.
Metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen: 2K(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2KOH(aq) + H₂(g).
Metal + chlorine → metal chloride (white solid): 2Li(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2LiCl(s).
The hydroxide solutions are alkaline: universal indicator turns purple.
Alkali metals are soft, have low densities and low melting points, which decrease down the group.
They are stored under oil because they react with oxygen and water in the air.
Down the group, the outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.

keyTerms.definition: The elements in Group 1 of the periodic table, which react with water to form alkaline hydroxide solutions.
The highest occupied energy level of an atom; Group 1 atoms have one electron in it.
The reduction in attraction between the nucleus and outer electrons caused by inner shells of electrons in between.
A compound containing hydroxide ions (OH⁻), such as NaOH, formed when an alkali metal reacts with water.
When a shiny metal surface becomes dull because it reacts with oxygen in the air to form an oxide layer.
A charged particle formed when an atom loses or gains electrons; Group 1 atoms form 1+ ions.
Loss of electrons; Group 1 metals are oxidised when they react: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻.

equations.name: Reaction with water (general)
equations.formula: alkali metal + water → metal hydroxide + hydrogen

workedExamples.title: Writing a balanced symbol equation
workedExamples.question: Write a balanced symbol equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of potassium with water.
steps: Word equation: potassium + water → potassium hydroxide + hydrogen.
Formulae: K, H₂O, KOH (K⁺ and OH⁻), H₂.
Unbalanced: K + H₂O → KOH + H₂. There are 2 H on the right in H₂ plus 1 in KOH, so 3 H on the right.
Put 2 in front of H₂O and KOH: K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂. Now put 2 in front of K.
Check: 2 K, 4 H and 2 O on each side. Add state symbols.

workedExamples.title: Using conservation of mass
workedExamples.question: 4.6 g of sodium reacts completely with 7.1 g of chlorine. Calculate the mass of sodium chloride formed.
steps: Mass is conserved in a chemical reaction: mass of products = mass of reactants.

workedExamples.title: Predicting a property from a trend
workedExamples.question: The melting points of potassium and caesium are 63 °C and 28 °C. Rubidium is between them. Estimate the melting point of rubidium by taking the mean of these values.
steps: Check: the estimate is between 28 and 63, as the trend (decreasing down the group) requires.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think potassium is more reactive because it has more outer electrons than sodium.
misconceptions.right: In fact all Group 1 atoms have one outer electron. Potassium is more reactive because its outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often think the greater nuclear charge down the group makes the outer electron harder to remove.
misconceptions.right: In fact the extra shells (distance and shielding) outweigh the increase in nuclear charge, so the attraction on the outer electron gets weaker.

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write the gas formed with water as oxygen, or the product as sodium oxide.
misconceptions.right: In fact the products are a metal hydroxide (such as NaOH) and hydrogen gas (H₂).

misconceptions.wrong: Students often write the formula of hydrogen gas as H.
misconceptions.right: In fact hydrogen gas is made of molecules, H₂, which is why the equations need balancing with 2s.

realWorld: Lithium is used in rechargeable lithium-ion batteries in phones and electric cars, partly because it has a very low density.
Sodium chloride (common salt) is used to season and preserve food and to grit icy roads.
Sodium vapour gives the yellow-orange glow of older street lamps.
Sodium hydroxide, made from salt, is used to make soap, paper and bleach.
higherTier: Ionic equation for the reaction with water: 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2Na⁺(aq) + 2OH⁻(aq) + H₂(g).
Half equation showing the metal being oxidised (loss of electrons): Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ (for potassium: K → K⁺ + e⁻).
In the reaction with chlorine, sodium atoms are oxidised (lose electrons) and chlorine atoms are reduced (gain electrons): Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻.
examTips: For reactivity trends, use all three ideas: outer electron further from the nucleus, more shielding by inner shells, weaker attraction so the electron is lost more easily.
Talk about 'the outer electron' (singular) for Group 1, and say it is 'lost', not 'gained' or 'shared'.
When describing observations, give things you would see (fizzing, melting into a ball, moving, lilac flame, getting smaller), not just 'hydrogen is produced'.
Learn the three general equations and check balancing: 2M + 2H₂O → 2MOH + H₂; 4M + O₂ → 2M₂O; 2M + Cl₂ → 2MCl.
summary: Group 1 alkali metals have one outer electron and form 1+ ions.
They react with water to give a hydroxide and hydrogen, with oxygen to give oxides, and with chlorine to give white chlorides.
The outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded down the group, so it is lost more easily.
Melting points decrease down the group; the metals are soft with low densities.
Trends can be used to predict the properties of rubidium and caesium.

questions.question: How many electrons are in the outer shell of a Group 1 atom?
questions.explanation: All alkali metal atoms have one outer electron; the group number tells you this.

questions.question: Which gas is produced when sodium reacts with water?
questions.explanation: Sodium + water → sodium hydroxide + hydrogen. The hydrogen comes from the water.

questions.question: How does the reactivity of the alkali metals change going down Group 1?
questions.explanation: Potassium is more reactive than sodium, which is more reactive than lithium.

questions.question: Why are lithium, sodium and potassium stored under oil?
options: To make them softer to cut
To keep them shiny for display
To stop them reacting with oxygen and water in the air
markScheme: 1 mark: stop reaction with oxygen and water (air)
questions.explanation: Alkali metals react quickly with oxygen and water vapour. Oil keeps the air away.

questions.question: Which statement about the alkali metals is correct?
options: They are hard metals with high densities
They are soft metals that can be cut with a knife
They have very high melting points
markScheme: 1 mark: soft, can be cut with a knife
questions.explanation: Alkali metals are soft, have low melting points, and lithium, sodium and potassium float on water.

questions.question: What colour does universal indicator turn after sodium has reacted with water?
questions.explanation: Sodium hydroxide is a strong alkali, so the solution has a high pH and universal indicator turns purple.

questions.question: Which observation is seen only when potassium, not lithium, is added to water?
options: Bubbles of gas are given off
The hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame
questions.explanation: All three metals float, fizz and get smaller. Potassium reacts so vigorously that the hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame.

questions.question: What is the formula of the oxide formed when lithium burns in oxygen?
questions.explanation: Lithium forms Li⁺ and oxide is O²⁻, so two lithium ions balance one oxide ion. LiOH is lithium hydroxide, formed with water.

questions.question: Which is the correctly balanced equation for the reaction of sodium with chlorine?
questions.explanation: Chlorine is diatomic (Cl₂), and sodium chloride is NaCl, so two sodium atoms react with one chlorine molecule.

questions.question: Why is potassium more reactive than sodium?
options: Potassium has more electrons in its outer shell
Potassium's outer electron is further from the nucleus and more shielded, so it is lost more easily
Potassium's larger nuclear charge attracts electrons from other atoms more strongly
Potassium has a lower density than sodium
markScheme: 1 mark: outer electron further from nucleus / more shielded / lost more easily
questions.explanation: Both have one outer electron. Distance and shielding outweigh the larger nuclear charge, so potassium loses its electron more easily.

questions.question: Caesium is near the bottom of Group 1. Which prediction about caesium is most likely to be correct?
options: It reacts explosively with water to form caesium hydroxide and hydrogen
It has a higher melting point than lithium
It does not react with chlorine
questions.explanation: Reactivity increases and melting point decreases down the group. All Group 1 metals form 1+ ions and react with chlorine.

questions.question: Which half equation shows what happens to sodium atoms when sodium reacts with water?
questions.explanation: Sodium atoms lose one electron to form Na⁺; loss of electrons is oxidation. The electron must appear on the right-hand side.

questions.question: How many electrons are in a potassium ion, K⁺? (Potassium has an atomic number of 19.)
questions.explanation: A potassium atom has 19 electrons. It loses one to form K⁺, leaving 18 (2,8,8).

questions.question: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of lithium oxide, Li₂O. (Ar: Li = 7, O = 16)
questions.explanation: There are two lithium atoms: 14 + 16 = 30.

questions.question: Calculate the relative formula mass (Mr) of potassium hydroxide, KOH. (Ar: K = 39, O = 16, H = 1)
questions.explanation: Add the relative atomic masses of one of each atom: 39 + 16 + 1 = 56.

questions.question: 2.3 g of sodium reacts completely with 3.55 g of chlorine. Calculate the mass of sodium chloride produced.
questions.explanation: No atoms are lost or made, so the mass of product equals the total mass of reactants: 2.3 + 3.55 = 5.85 g.

questions.question: The melting point of potassium is 63 °C and the melting point of caesium is 28 °C. Estimate the melting point of rubidium, which lies between them, by calculating the mean of the two values.
questions.explanation: 91 ÷ 2 = 45.5 °C. The real value is 39 °C, so the estimate is reasonable but the trend is not perfectly regular.

questions.question:
Calculate the mass of hydrogen produced when 0.46 g of sodium reacts with excess water.
2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g)
(Ar: Na = 23, H = 1)
questions.explanation: The equation shows 2 mol Na gives 1 mol H₂. Mr of H₂ is 2. A common error is forgetting to halve the moles.

questions.question: State why the Group 1 elements are called the alkali metals.
acceptedAnswers: react with water to form alkaline solutions
markScheme: 1 mark: they react with water to form alkaline solutions (hydroxides)
questions.explanation: The metal hydroxides formed with water are alkalis.

questions.question: A small piece of sodium is added to a trough of water. Describe two things you would see.
markScheme: 1 mark each for any two: floats / fizzes or bubbles / melts into a ball / moves around on the surface / gets smaller and disappears
questions.explanation: 'Hydrogen is produced' is not an observation; you would see fizzing.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation, including state symbols, for the reaction of potassium with water.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct formulae and balancing: 2K + 2H₂O → 2KOH + H₂
questions.explanation: Hydrogen is diatomic, so two potassium atoms and two water molecules are needed.

questions.question: Write a balanced symbol equation, including state symbols, for the reaction of lithium with oxygen.
markScheme: 1 mark: correct formulae Li, O₂, Li₂O and balancing 4 : 1 : 2
questions.explanation: Li₂O contains two lithium atoms, and oxygen is O₂, so 4 lithium atoms make 2 Li₂O.

questions.question: A freshly cut piece of sodium is shiny, but after a few seconds in air the surface becomes dull. Explain why.
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium reacts with oxygen in the air
1 mark: forming a (dull) layer of sodium oxide on the surface
questions.explanation: This is tarnishing. It happens faster for potassium because it is more reactive.

questions.question: Explain why all the Group 1 elements have similar chemical properties.
markScheme: 1 mark: all have one electron in the outer shell
1 mark: so they all react by losing one electron to form 1+ ions
questions.explanation: Chemical properties depend on outer electrons, so elements with the same outer shell arrangement behave similarly.

questions.question: Rubidium is below potassium in Group 1. Predict the formula of rubidium chloride and describe what it would look like at room temperature.
questions.explanation: Rubidium forms Rb⁺ and chlorine forms Cl⁻, so the formula is RbCl, a white ionic solid like NaCl and KCl.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of atomic structure, why reactivity increases going down Group 1.
markScheme: 1 mark: going down, atoms have more shells, so the outer electron is further from the nucleus
1 mark: there is more shielding from inner electrons, so the attraction between the nucleus and the outer electron is weaker
1 mark: so the outer electron is lost more easily
questions.explanation: All three steps are needed: distance or shielding, weaker attraction, and easier loss of the electron.

questions.question: Write the ionic equation, with state symbols, for the reaction of sodium with water, and explain why sodium is described as being oxidised.
markScheme: 1 mark: sodium atoms lose electrons (Na → Na⁺ + e⁻), and loss of electrons is oxidation
questions.explanation: Sodium hydroxide is ionic and dissolves, so in the ionic equation it is written as separate Na⁺ and OH⁻ ions.

questions.question: Describe what you would see when lithium, sodium and potassium are each added to water. Include a balanced symbol equation for one of the reactions, and explain the trend in reactivity.
markScheme: Indicative content: all float, fizz (hydrogen), get smaller and form an alkaline solution (universal indicator turns purple); lithium fizzes steadily and slowly disappears; sodium melts into a ball, fizzes rapidly and moves around; potassium melts, fizzes violently, hydrogen ignites with a lilac flame; equation, for example 2Na(s) + 2H₂O(l) → 2NaOH(aq) + H₂(g); reactivity increases down the group; atoms have more shells, outer electron further from the nucleus; more shielding; weaker attraction; outer electron lost more easily.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): detailed, correct observations for all three metals, a correct balanced equation, and a full explanation of the trend in terms of electrons.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): observations for at least two metals with a comparison, a mostly correct equation or partial explanation.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some correct observations or a statement of the trend with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Compare the metals directly (more vigorous, faster) and link the trend to the outer electron being lost more easily.

questions.question:
A student made these predictions about francium, the element at the bottom of Group 1:
1. Francium will have a higher melting point than caesium.
2. Francium will react with water to form francium hydroxide, FrOH, and hydrogen.
3. Francium will form Fr²⁺ ions.
4. Francium will be the most reactive alkali metal.
Evaluate each prediction, using trends in Group 1.
markScheme: Indicative content: prediction 1 is incorrect, since melting points decrease down the group, so francium would have a lower melting point than caesium; prediction 2 is correct, since all alkali metals react with water to form a hydroxide MOH and hydrogen; prediction 3 is incorrect, since francium has one outer electron so forms Fr⁺ ions; prediction 4 is correct, since reactivity increases down the group because the outer electron is furthest from the nucleus, most shielded, so most easily lost.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): all four predictions correctly judged with reasons based on trends or electronic structure.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): some predictions correctly judged with limited reasons.
questions.explanation: Evaluating means judging each prediction as right or wrong and giving a reason from the group trends.

questions.question:
Sodium reacts with chlorine to form sodium chloride, and potassium reacts with chlorine more vigorously to form potassium chloride.
Explain these reactions in terms of electron transfer. Include half equations and a balanced symbol equation, and explain why potassium reacts more vigorously.
markScheme: Indicative content: 2Na(s) + Cl₂(g) → 2NaCl(s) (or 2K + Cl₂ → 2KCl); each sodium atom loses its one outer electron: Na → Na⁺ + e⁻ (oxidation); each chlorine molecule gains two electrons: Cl₂ + 2e⁻ → 2Cl⁻ (reduction); ions have noble gas electronic structures (Na⁺ 2,8; Cl⁻ 2,8,8); oppositely charged ions attract to form an ionic compound; potassium's outer electron is further from the nucleus (extra shell) and more shielded; attraction to the nucleus weaker; electron lost more easily, so potassium reacts more vigorously.
Level 3 (5 to 6 marks): correct equations and half equations, clear description of electron transfer with oxidation and reduction, and a full explanation of the difference in reactivity.
Level 2 (3 to 4 marks): electron transfer described with at least one correct equation or half equation, and some explanation of reactivity.
Level 1 (1 to 2 marks): simple statements, for example 'sodium loses an electron', with little explanation.
questions.explanation: Use OIL RIG: oxidation is loss, reduction is gain of electrons. The vigour depends on how easily the metal loses its outer electron.
